To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

IL-3 can regulate cell cycle progression of myeloid and lymphoid precursor cells, and that the ability of other CSFs to regulate the growth of these cells depends upon both the lineage from which they were cloned and the phase of the cycle in which the cells reside.
IL-3 is both a competence and a progression factor for IL-3-dependent cells.
the ability of various hematopoeitic growth factors to regulate growth and differentiation of hematopoietic progenitor clones is dependent upon the phase of the cycle in which those clones reside.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms that regulate hematopoiesis.
the molecular mechanisms by which hematopoietic cells respond to the growth factors that control their proliferation and differentiation.
the mechanisms by which hematopoietic progenitor cells respond to growth factors and cytokines.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the growth of hematopoietic progenitor cells is a complex and highly regulated process, which requires the interaction of a variety of growth factors.
the ability of CSFs to regulate cell proliferation and differentiation is cell lineage- and cell cycle-dependent.
the cell cycle is a critical factor in determining the biological activities of various hematopoetic growth factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
IL-3 is the most potent growth factor for the FDC-P1 clone, whereas G/M-CSF is the most potent for the F15.12 clone.

IL-3 can be considered as a "master growth factor," which can induce growth and/or differentiation of a number of hematopoietic progenitors, whereas G/M-CSF is more lineage restricted and can only induce the differentiation and proliferation of progenitors belonging to the myeloid lineage.
the ability of CSFs to regulate the cell cycle of a hematopoietic clone is lineage dependent and cell cycle stage dependent.
The main takeaway from our work is that

IL-3, G/M-CSf and IL-4 all can be progression factors, and that they can act as competence factors only in defined points of the cell cycle, and that the lineage from which the cell was derived will determine whether the factor will be a progression or competence factor.
IL-3 can be a progression factor for some clones, a competence factor for others, and a combination of both in still others.
hematopoietic cell growth factor requirements are cell cycle stage specific.
